response.query: Which standardized error taxonomy and severity rubric (e.g., IFCC/NCCLS-adapted) will we use to classify pre-analytical, analytical, and post-analytical errors consistently across the three-year dataset?
response.answer: We will use the IFCC/NCCLS-adapted taxonomy for classifying pre-analytical, analytical, and post-analytical errors consistently. This taxonomy includes standardized quality indicators for error assessment.

results.content: There are a variety of free on-line resources available to aid in managing the extra-analytical phase and the recent publication of quality indicators and proposed performance levels by the International Federation of Clinical Chemistry and Laboratory Medicine (IFCC) working group on laboratory errors and patient safety provides particularly useful benchmarking data. Medical Errors: Pre-Analytical Issue in Patient Safety The last few decades have seen a significant decrease in the rates of analytical errors in clinical laboratories, while a growing body of evidence demonstrates that the pre- and post-analytical steps of the total testing process (TTP) are more error-prone than the analytical phase.

results.title: A look at pre-analytical error rates, 2014 - Westgard QC
results.content: ## A look at pre-analytical error rates, 2014. **A new study looks at the frequency of errors in laboratory processes across the Total Testing Process. The study covers pre-analytical error rates from 2011 at the County Emergency Clinical Hospital in Timisoara, Romania. This recent study looked at seven of the quality indicators that are approved by the IFCC working group on "Laboratory Errors and Patienty Safety" (WG-LEPS), concentrating on quality indicators in the pre-analytical phase. | **Laboratory Process, 2011** | **Defect rate** | **Sigma-metric (short-term)** |. Except that sodium assay, which at 3.5 Sigma (short-term) is going to generate a lot of errors (22,750 defects-per-million). If we add up all the pre-analytical errors that they found, it totals 1,457 errors, or about 0.86% or 3.8 on the short-term Sigma scale. That sodium method could be generating more than twice the defects of all the pre-analytical errors *combined*. For years, we have been told the opposite, that analytical methods are all great and we only need to focus on the pre-analytical errors.

results.title: Evaluation of Laboratory Performance in Consideration with Pre analytical and Post analytical Quality Indicators - PMC
results.content: Hence, with the aim to achieve greater standardization and quality of the operational procedures, this study was conducted to quantify performance in the extra-analytical phase of TTP in Clinical Biochemistry laboratory using various quality indicators (QIs). To monitor process performance of laboratory services, set of QIs related to critical processes are defined and recommended by the International Federation of Clinical Chemistry (IFCC) and Laboratory Medicine Working Group on Laboratory Errors and Patient Safety (WGLEPS) [10]; as tabulated in Tables 1 and 2 for pre- and post-analytical phase of TTP [10]. For assessment of pre-analytical phase, quality indicator one each from the unsuitable samples for transportation and storage problems (% of number of suitable samples not received; QI-8), incorrect sample type (% of number of samples received in inappropriate container; QI-9), hemolysed sample (% of number of samples hemolysed; QI-10), incorrect fill level (% of number of samples with inadequate sample volume; QI 12) and test transcription errors (% of number of samples received mismatched; QI 15) were selected, to quantify the degree to which set targets are attained. To mitigate the systematic or random errors (for example, facilities using wrong form/incorrect type of blood tube is systematic error and a staff who has made a mistake in using wrong tube/filling in wrong information is random error) in clinical laboratories, espousal of QIs aids as a means to measure and evaluate the quality and effectiveness of laboratory testing i.e., QIs serves as an error reduction tool (4–9). In this study, set of QIs were assessed in terms of frequency and type of errors for certain critical processes related to extra-analytical phase by screening all the samples processed in clinical Biochemistry laboratory and indeed found a significant acceptable performance levels in different ranges for majority of studied quality indicators (Table 5). The other pre-analytical error which was found to be in unacceptable limit as per the IFCC guidelines of quality specifications was correct sample not received, with error rate of 0.90% of all samples covered in the study, accounting for 24.18% of total pre-analytical errors.
